questions.title: Did the Board have to use the same 'similarity of goods/services' scope for DuPont factor six as it used for factor two?
questions.question_body: The Board found under factor two that Apex's 'banking and financing services' are highly similar to CC Serve's 'credit card services,' even 'legally identical, in part.' But for factor six, it limited the relevant public to 'consumers of credit card services' and treated Aspire uses for other banking/financing services as 'essentially irrelevant.' The Federal Circuit says that was legal error because factor six, like factor two, deals with 'similar' goods/services. Does 'similar' need to be defined consistently across the DuPont factors once the Board has made a finding under factor two, or can the Board legitimately narrow the scope for factor six? How should the Board decide the proper scope of 'similar' goods/services for the crowded-field analysis when it has already found a high degree of similarity under factor two?

questions.title: What legal effect does deletion of 'credit card services' from the USPTO ID Manual have on interpreting CC Serve’s 1998 identification?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes the 'credit card services' entry was deleted from the Trademark ID Manual after CC Serve’s registration. The Board then used dictionaries to construe 'credit card services' broadly (issuing cards, processing transactions, account management, monitoring, etc.). Does removal of a term from the ID Manual have any retroactive effect on an existing registration’s scope? Is the ID Manual binding or merely persuasive when construing legacy identifications? Are there cases on how to interpret vague or outdated identifications when the Manual has changed, and what sources (dictionaries, industry usage, prosecution history) are appropriate?

questions.title: In a §2(d) opposition, why did the TTAB compare the identifications rather than Apex’s actual services (it doesn’t issue credit cards)?
questions.question_body: Apex says it does not offer credit cards; it runs retail banking and planned an online bank. The Board nevertheless treated Apex’s 'banking and financing services' as encompassing credit card issuance/credit extension, concluding the services are 'legally identical, in part.' I thought likelihood-of-confusion analysis considers real-world marketplace conditions. Why didn’t Apex’s actual non-offering of credit cards matter? Is there a rule that the TTAB compares services as identified in the application/registration regardless of actual use, and could Apex have narrowed its identification (e.g., with limitations) to avoid overlap? How do channel-of-trade presumptions play into this?

questions.title: How many third-party 'Aspire' uses are needed to show weakness, and do registrations versus marketplace uses carry different weight?
questions.question_body: The Board counted nine Aspire-formative marks for credit card services and held that was not 'considerable' or 'ubiquitous' enough to show weakness (citing Jack Wolfskin and Juice Generation). Apex pointed to 42 additional Aspire uses in broader financial services, which the Board disregarded but the Federal Circuit says should be reconsidered. Is there any benchmark for how much third-party evidence establishes a 'crowded field,' or is it entirely context-specific? Do third-party registrations have the same probative value as evidence of actual marketplace use when assessing conceptual and/or commercial weakness?

questions.title: How does factor six’s strength/weakness finding influence factor one’s 'commercial impression' analysis?
questions.question_body: The court vacated factor one because a different determination on factor six (third-party use/strength) could change the marks’ 'overall commercial impression.' Do tribunals fold a mark’s conceptual/commercial strength into the factor-one similarity analysis (appearance, sound, connotation, commercial impression), or is 'strength' supposed to be assessed under separate DuPont factors? Practically, if ASPIRE is found weak in financial services on remand, how would that affect whether adding 'BANK' to ASPIRE meaningfully changes the commercial impression and reduces likely confusion?

questions.title: Does CC Serve’s partnering with issuing banks affect whether it really offers 'credit card services' for §2(d) purposes?
questions.question_body: CC Serve partners with a bank that issues ASPIRE-branded cards and accounts, while CC Serve services the accounts and manages the program. Apex argues CC Serve is 'not providing banking services' itself. For priority and similarity-of-services, does providing program-management/servicing under the mark qualify as 'credit card services' even if a partner bank is the legal issuer? Is this analyzed under the 'related company' doctrine (Lanham Act §1055) or quality/control principles, and does it affect the second DuPont factor analysis?

questions.title: Why could the Federal Circuit affirm factor two on 'substantial evidence' but vacate factor six as a 'legal error'?
questions.question_body: The court reviews legal conclusions de novo and factual findings for substantial evidence. It affirmed the Board’s factor-two finding (high similarity of services) as supported by substantial evidence, but vacated factor six because the Board applied an unduly narrow legal standard for 'similar' goods/services. How do we draw the line between a factual finding supported by substantial evidence and a legal error in applying the correct standard within the DuPont framework? Did the Federal Circuit reweigh factor-six evidence, or did it just correct the legal framework and remand for the Board to reweigh?

questions.title: On remand, can the TTAB consider more third-party 'Aspire' evidence, or is it limited to the existing record?
questions.question_body: This was a direct appeal to the Federal Circuit on the existing TTAB record. The court vacated and remanded for reconsideration of factors six and one. Procedurally, can the TTAB reopen the record to allow additional third-party use/registration evidence beyond the nine credit-card uses the Board counted, or is the Board generally constrained to the current record and just required to reassess it under the correct legal standard? If reopening is possible, under what authority and subject to what limitations?
